{{Short description|Branch of mathematics}}
{{Lie groups}}
In [[mathematics]], a [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is '''nilpotent''' if its lower central series terminates in the zero subalgebra. The ''lower central series'' is the sequence of subalgebras

:<math> \mathfrak{g} \supseteq [\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}] \supseteq [\mathfrak{g},[\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}]] \supseteq [\mathfrak{g},[\mathfrak{g},[\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}]]] \supseteq ...</math>

We write <math>\mathfrak{g}_0 = \mathfrak{g}</math>, and <math>\mathfrak{g}_n = [\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}_{n-1}]</math> for all <math>n > 0</math>. If the lower central series eventually arrives at the zero subalgebra, then the Lie algebra is called nilpotent. The lower central series for Lie algebras is analogous to the [[lower central series]] in [[group theory]], and nilpotent Lie algebras are analogs of [[nilpotent group]]s.

The nilpotent Lie algebras are precisely those that can be obtained from abelian Lie algebras, by successive [[central extension (mathematics)|central extension]]s.

Note that the definition means that, viewed as a non-associative non-unital algebra, a Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is nilpotent if it is nilpotent as an ideal.

== Definition ==
Let <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> be a [[Lie algebra]]. One says that <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is '''nilpotent''' if the [[lower central series]] terminates, i.e. if <math>\mathfrak{g}_n = 0</math>  for some <math>n\in\mathbb{N}.</math>

Explicitly, this means that
:<math>[X_1, [X_2,[\cdots[X_{n}, Y]\cdots]] = \mathrm{ad}_{X_1}\mathrm{ad}_{X_2}\cdots\mathrm{ad}_{X_{n}}Y = 0</math> 
::::::<math>\forall X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_{n}, Y \in \mathfrak{g},\qquad(1)</math>
so that {{math|ad<sub>''X''<sub>1</sub></sub>ad<sub>''X''<sub>2</sub></sub> ⋅⋅⋅ ad<sub>''X''<sub>''n''</sub></sub> {{=}} 0}}.

== Equivalent conditions==

A very special consequence of (1) is that
:<math>[X, [X,[\cdots[X, Y]\cdots] = {\mathrm{ad}_X}^{n}Y \in \mathfrak{g}_n = 0 \quad \forall X, Y \in \mathfrak{g}.\qquad(2)</math>
Thus {{math|(ad<sub>''X''</sub>)<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} 0}} for all <math>X \in \mathfrak{g}</math>.  That is, {{math|ad<sub>''X''</sub>}} is a [[nilpotent|nilpotent endomorphism]] in the usual sense of linear endomorphisms (rather than of Lie algebras). We call such an element {{math|''X''}} in <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> '''ad-nilpotent'''.

Remarkably, if <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is finite dimensional, the apparently much weaker condition (2) is actually equivalent to (1), as stated by

:'' [[Engel's theorem]]: A finite dimensional Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is nilpotent if and only if all elements of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> are ad-nilpotent,''

which we will not prove here.

A somewhat easier equivalent condition for the nilpotency of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> :  <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is nilpotent if and only if <math>\mathrm{ad} \, \mathfrak{g}</math> is nilpotent (as a Lie algebra). To see this, first observe that (1) implies that <math>\mathrm{ad} \, \mathfrak{g}</math> is nilpotent, since the expansion of an {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-fold nested bracket will consist of terms of the form in (1). Conversely, one may write<ref>{{harvnb|Knapp|2002}} Proposition 1.32.</ref>
:<math>[[\cdots[X_{n},X_{n-1}],\cdots,X_2],X_1] = \mathrm{ad}[\cdots[X_{n},X_{n-1}], \cdots, X_2](X_1),</math>
and since {{math|ad}} is a Lie algebra homomorphism,
:<math>\begin{align}\mathrm{ad}[\cdots[X_{n},X_{n-1}], \cdots, X_2] &= [\mathrm{ad}[\cdots[X_{n},X_{n-1}],\cdots X_3], \mathrm{ad}_{X_2}]\\
 &= \ldots = [\cdots[\mathrm{ad}_{X_{n}}, \mathrm{ad}_{X_{n-1}}], \cdots \mathrm{ad}_{X_2}].\end{align}</math>
If <math>\mathrm{ad} \, \mathfrak{g}</math> is nilpotent, the last expression is zero for large enough ''n'', and accordingly the first. But this implies (1), so <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is nilpotent.

Also, a finite-dimensional Lie algebra is nilpotent if and only if there exists a descending chain of ideals <math>\mathfrak g = \mathfrak g_0 \supset \mathfrak g_1 \supset \cdots \supset \mathfrak g_n = 0</math> such that <math>[\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g_i] \subset \mathfrak g_{i+1}</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Serre|loc=Ch. I, Proposition 1.}}</ref>

== Examples ==

=== Strictly upper triangular matrices ===
If <math>\mathfrak{gl}(k,\mathbb R)</math> is the set of {{math|''k × k''}} matrices with entries in <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, then the [[subalgebra]] consisting of strictly [[upper triangular matrices]] is a nilpotent Lie algebra.

=== Heisenberg algebras ===
A [[Heisenberg algebra]] is nilpotent. For example, in dimension 3, the commutator of two matrices<blockquote><math>\left[ \begin{bmatrix}
0 & a & b \\
0 & 0 & c \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix} , 
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & a' & b' \\
0 & 0 & c' \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\right]
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0 & a'' \\
0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
</math></blockquote>where <math>a'' = ac' - a'c</math>.

=== Cartan subalgebras ===
A [[Cartan subalgebra]] <math>\mathfrak{c}</math> of a [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{l}</math> is nilpotent and [[self-normalizing]]<ref>{{Cite book|last=Humphreys, James E.|title=Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory|date=1972|publisher=Springer New York|isbn=978-1-4612-6398-2|location=New York, NY|oclc=852791600}}</ref> <sup>page 80</sup>. The self-normalizing condition is equivalent to being the normalizer of a Lie algebra. This means <math>\mathfrak{c} = N_\mathfrak{l}(\mathfrak{c}) = \{ x \in \mathfrak{l} : [x,c] \subset \mathfrak{c} \text{ for } c \in \mathfrak{c} \}</math>. This includes all diagonal matrices <math>\mathfrak{d}(n)</math> in <math>\mathfrak{gl}(n)</math>.

=== Other examples ===
If a [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> has an [[automorphism]] of prime period with no fixed points except at {{math|0}}, then <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is nilpotent.<ref>{{Citation|last=Jacobson|first=N.|author-link=Nathan Jacobson|chapter=A Note on Automorphisms and Derivations of Lie Algebras|date=1989|title=Nathan Jacobson Collected Mathematical Papers: Volume 2 (1947–1965)|pages=251–253|editor-last=Jacobson|editor-first=Nathan|series=Contemporary Mathematicians|publisher=Birkhäuser|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-3694-8_16|isbn=978-1-4612-3694-8}}</ref>

== Properties ==

=== Nilpotent Lie algebras are solvable ===
Every nilpotent Lie algebra is [[Solvable Lie algebra|solvable]]. This is useful in proving the solvability of a [[Lie algebra]] since, in practice, it is usually easier to prove nilpotency (when it holds!) rather than solvability. However, in general, the converse of this property is false. For example, the subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak{gl}(k,\mathbb R)</math> ({{math|''k'' ≥ 2}}) consisting of upper triangular matrices, <math>\mathfrak{b}(k,\mathbb R)</math>, is solvable but not nilpotent.

=== Subalgebras and images ===
If a [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is nilpotent, then all [[subalgebra]]s and homomorphic images are nilpotent.

=== Nilpotency of the quotient by the center ===
If the [[quotient Lie algebra|quotient algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g}/Z(\mathfrak g)</math>, where <math>Z(\mathfrak{g})</math> is the [[Center (algebra)|center]] of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, is nilpotent, then so is <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. This is to say that a central extension of a nilpotent Lie algebra by a nilpotent Lie algebra is nilpotent.

=== Engel's theorem ===
[[Engel's theorem]]: A finite dimensional Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is nilpotent if and only if all elements of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> are ad-nilpotent.

=== Zero Killing form ===
The [[Killing form]] of a nilpotent Lie algebra is {{math|0}}.

=== Have outer automorphisms ===
A nonzero nilpotent Lie algebra has an [[outer automorphism]], that is, an automorphism that is not in the image of Ad.

=== Derived subalgebras of solvable Lie algebras ===
The [[solvable Lie algebra|derived subalgebra]] of a finite dimensional solvable Lie algebra over a field of characteristic 0 is nilpotent.
